cues.en: So what is performance?
Now when we think about performance in the context of a web site we're visiting, performance can be a
lot of different things
but I think there are two main categories into which we can split this term performance.
We can have a look at the startup time of a web site, of a web application and we can have a look at
the runtime performance because these are really two different things that of course in the end work
together end and which both matter. Startup time is all about the question how long does it take to see something
on the screen and how quickly is a user able to interact with the page,
we all know how it feels like when we visit a page which is slow, which takes forever to load or which
at some point seems like it loaded
but when we try to click something, nothing happens,
so we all know that and therefore this is of course one important part. But then once a page did load, of course
it should also offer a great performance and also avoid certain bugs.
Here the question is how is smooth the application runs in general,
does it occasionally freeze or lag?
We of course don't like visiting pages where we for example try to enter some text into a text box and
it takes us forever to do so because our input is only picked up with a lag, especially web sites or
web applications, I use these terms interchangeably as you can tell, with a lot of animations could
end up in a state where we have a lot of visual lag, a lot of visual change where the animations don't
play smoothly or anything like that or where a running animation prevents us from doing anything else
or of course we could have a web site with certain memory leaks which add up over time,
so where some part of the code is buggy and actually occupies more and more memory the more often it
runs and depending on the device you're running this website on, eventually the device or the page might
run out of memory and the browser might shut it down therefore,
so that of course is also something we want avoid but it's also important to understand that performance
is not just about Javascript but about everything that's involved when it comes to visiting and
using a web page.
It's influenced by a lot of factors, the CSS code and HTML code also play a role.
If you have very complex CSS selectors, that takes the browser longer to apply styling. If you have a
lot of unnecessary HTML code, that is more code which needs to be downloaded initially hence slowing
down the startup time
but of course Javascript is a major factor because that influences a lot of the parts related to runtime
performance
and if you're downloading a lot of Javascript code, it of course also influences the startup time negatively.
Also of course the speed of the server you're hosting your web site on, as well as the configuration
of the server can have a negative impact on your users.
If you have a server that resides in the US and you have a lot of users from let's say India,
well it simply takes you a bit longer to get your data from the server.
Now of course we're talking about milliseconds here and it might not really have an impact
but the bigger your application is, the more users you're reaching, the more you want to think about all
the factors that influence performance or that could potentially influence performance and optimize
them.
In this module however, I will focus on the Javascript performance part but I want to put that out
there that there are other factors which also play a role.
Now when we talk about Javascript performance, what influences our performance there? When we think about
our Javascript execution,
of course here again we have two different areas,
we have the startup time,
the question here is how fast the script loads and is able to execute and we have the runtime performance
and here it's all about the work
the script has to do and how efficiently it does that work
and it's not just about the work the script does on its own but also about the interactions with our
other web page,
when you work with the DOM for example, when you add and remove HTML elements via Javascript, that can
have a negative impact on the overall web application performance
if you doing this in a poor way and I'll come back to that in this module and of course we have this
memory thing. You want to avoid memory leaks to make sure that you're not slowing down the application
over time or that you even have the worst case scenario of the browser shutting down your application.
Now also it's important to understand that I talked about the browser here,
I talked about the DOM but of course Javascript as you'll learned does not just run in the browser.
Now the startup time, that's really a thing that is primarily related to the browser side because when
we're talking about server side Javascript with Node.js, then there is no download delay or anything
like that,
The code already is on the server where it will get executed,
so that whole startup time thing is less of an issue on the server side because all the code is already
there
so therefore it can be executed very efficiently and quickly by default.
But when we talk about runtime performance, that affects all Javascript environments, all places where
we can execute Javascript.
Of course there are certain problems which can only occur in the browser,
for example when we talk about DOM interaction but there also are other parts, other things about Javascript
which apply to both browser side and server side Javascript.
In this modular, I will focus on the browser side because there we actually have more pitfalls but we'll
also have a look at certain things which you will see really affect any Javascript code no matter where
it runs.
So we have these different layers of performance optimization we could say, we have the startup time and
the runtime
and now let's have a look at the different things which affect performance there.
Now of course there are a lot of tiny factors which influence it but there are a couple of bigger categories
and potential improvements I'd like to think about when we have a look at these different layers. For
the startup time, an important factor is the size of our scripts,
so simply the question how big is our Javascript file
we're forcing the user to download before anything is able to happen on the page?
Remember when I said a couple of minutes ago that we have two parts when we think about startup time -
the time it takes to display something on the screen and the time it takes until the user is able to
do something with that screen,
well the script size can affect both.
If your script renders a lot of visual parts on the screen, then of course it affects how quickly the
user is able to see something on the screen but it most certainly will impact how quickly the user is
able to interact
because if your script is needed to add event listeners to a button and so on, then of course even if the button
is visible the user will not be able to do anything with it if your script hasn't finished downloading
yet and isn't available yet.
So therefore the script size, the size of the script file really plays an important role here,
the bigger it is the longer it takes users to download them and the longer it will take users to work
with your page and keep in mind that not every user is visiting your page from a great Internet connection.
Users might be using slow devices in slow network areas and therefore even a script file which is only
100kb big can take a couple of seconds to download and that could lead to a bad user experience.
Now besides the script size, it's also the amount of HTTP round trips and I covered this earlier
when we talked about Javascript modules and when we introduced webpack to bundle them into a single
or a few bundles
and the reason for a that is that
if we're working with a lot of script files and of course the same is true for a lot of CSS files
by the way, then the browser has to download all these files to make your page work and every
HttpRequest that needs to be sent to download something has a certain base cost it takes to set up that
request and send it, no matter how big the file is which you're downloading.
So the more HTTP round trips it takes to finally have the final state of your page, the longer
it will take until your page is ready to run and therefore
this is definitely a part you want to optimize and of course we already started optimizing both the
size and the number of HTTP round trips by adding webpack which does minify and optimize our code and which
also bundles our code together.
So now what about the runtime performance? There,
it's of course all about optimizing our code execution. If we're working in the browser environment,
that also includes one important aspect and that is DOM access,
so when we work with the DOM, when we add elements, when we remove elements, we want to avoid unnecessary
code execution, we want to write code which is efficient to execute and we definitely want to avoid unnecessary
DOM operations because if we unnecessarily for example re-render too many elements on the screen even
though maybe just one element needs to change, then we affect performance because it turns out working
with the DOM is really expensive
from a performance perspective because Javascript has to talk to the browser, the browser has to go through
the DOM and find the place you want to change, it then has to create a new element, it has to add the
element or remove one, whatever you're doing and that all are a lot of steps.
Now of course we're still talking about milliseconds here but they can really add up,
so being efficient here is super important as you will see in this module.
The other big factor are memory leaks, it's easy to introduce leaks and not all leaks are horrible, you
might not even recognize them
and I can tell you a lot of web pages out there do have tiny memory leaks but if you have bigger ones,
they can really add up and can lead to your page becoming slower or to actually even crash in the worst
case scenario. Now it's also interesting to think about different ways of solving one and the same problem
in Javascript,
so to find code alternatives with better performance. I will show an example for this throughout
this module. In the end here this is related to the first box here in the runtime performance part,
the code execution which we want to optimize. When you for example loop through an array, it turns out
you have a couple of different ways of doing so and they don't all have the same performance,
so that's also a thing you could think about and you could try to optimize. Related to that is another
approach which is called micro optimizations,
you can optimize certain parts of your code and actually looping through an array with a quicker alternative
would be one example for such a micro optimization, you can optimize parts of your code for specific use
cases. You could opt to use a certain data structure because it's a bit quicker than that other approach
you used before.
Now generally, you want to shy away from such micro optimizations though and I will come back to those
throughout the module and explain why you should be really careful when you try to optimize everything
but it is a thing which can matter in niche scenarios and very large applications,
the most important parts you want to care about are the first two boxes here in the runtime performance
part and of course all the boxes in the startup time performance part. And of course as mentioned, always
keep in mind that Javascript is just one part,
when we talk about optimizing our web page, it also includes things like writing efficient CSS and so
on
but that's simply not the focus of this course and Javascript typically is the most important thing to
optimize.
So with that we're almost done with the theory,
let's now find out how we can approach this whole performance optimization thing.
Now when you want to optimize your page, it's actually wrong to just go into the code and start changing
anything,
instead you want to measure and audit your page and find performance bottlenecks.
Don't guess, it's that measure.
You want to find out how many round trips you have, how big your script is which needs to be downloaded.
You maybe want to set certain budgets so that you know okay, my script has to be below 100kb and
if it is above it, I will do everything I can to shrink it.
So that's of course one important thing and you want to find out how big it is and how long it takes
before you start optimizing it.
You also want to measure the runtime performance with the help of browser dev tools.
There are a lot of useful features in modern browser dev tools which you can use to find out how long
certain parts of your script take and then you can find out if that seems too long to you,
you can try out an alternative and find out if that is actually better.
You can also explore best practices and patterns and benchmarks you find on the Internet,
you will find a lot of blog posts and discussions when you Google Javascript performance or even more
specific performance questions and you can then have a look at how other people are solving certain
problems or how they are approaching certain things,
so this can also be a useful thing to find out what you could look into
and also important because that is a common mistake, when you do measure performance, measure your production
ready code.
Don't do this in development mode because in development mode, your code is not optimal at all,
build tools like webpack where you use the webpack dev server inject a lot of extra code into your code
to enhance the debugging experience.
Now that's great for finding ordinary issues and problems but it's not great for measuring performance
because the performance during development will not be that great because it's simply not what matters
during development
but if you want to of course have great performance in production, so it's the production ready code
you should test.
Now when we talk about measuring performance, there are a couple of different ways of measuring it.
Now I mentioned the browser dev tools, you also can add certain code snippets to your code, to be precise
you can use performance now which is available in the browser to get a time snapshot and you can take
that before and after your running operation you're not sure about and this allows you to find out
how long an operation takes.
Then of course outside of your code, you do have the browser dev tools as I mentioned, where you have
many features that allow you to detect all kinds of different problems and bottlenecks you might have in
your code and you also have certain web sites like jsperf.com which allow you to benchmark certain
code alternatives against each other and find out which one is quicker.
You also have webpagetest.com, which is a site you can use to test a hosted web site, so not your
locally running one but a hosted web site and which then we'll give you a rich report on how that site
performed and what you could look into there.
Now these are just some tools and I can only recommend that you also Google web site performance,
Javascript performance to find more approaches and more tools that might work well for you.
